p: If you've never done an escape room, here's roughly how it goes. You'll arrive, check in and meet your game host, who'll explain the rules and the story behind your room. Most escape rooms ask you to leave phones and bags outside, so you can focus on the game without distractions. Then the door shuts, the clock starts, and it's over to you.

Inside, you'll search every nook and cranny for clues, padlocks, hidden compartments and codes. Some puzzles are logical, some are visual and some require a bit of lateral thinking. The host will be watching and can give you a hint if you're stuck, so don't be afraid to ask, because getting out with a hint still counts as a win in most people's books.

Picking the right team size makes a big difference. Too few people and you'll struggle to cover everything; too many and you'll be tripping over each other. Four to six players works well for most rooms, but ask the venue for their recommendation for your chosen theme. Mixing different skills helps too: someone who's good with numbers, someone with a sharp eye and someone who keeps everyone calm is a winning combination.

Afterwards, most groups enjoy a debrief, comparing notes on who spotted the crucial clue and who spent ten minutes trying to open a drawer that wasn't a puzzle at all. Game hosts often take a team photo at the end, which makes a fun keepsake for birthdays or work socials.
With four rooms, Game Over is a great place to come back to. Once you've conquered one, you can return with the same crew and try another, building your escape-room skills as you go.
